title: Sudo — The Superpower
objective: Understand the sudo command, the root user, and how to safely run commands with superuser privileges.
explanation: Every Linux system has a special user called root. Root is the superuser — the administrator who can do absolutely anything: install software, change system files, create or delete users, and even break the entire system. Because root is so powerful, you should never log in as root directly. Instead, Linux gives you a safer way to borrow root powers temporarily: the sudo command. Sudo stands for superuser do. When you put sudo in front of a command, Linux checks if you are allowed to use it, asks for your password, and then runs that command with root privileges. For example, updating your software list requires root access, so you type sudo apt update instead of just apt update. Your password is not shown as you type it — not even dots appear. This is normal and is a security feature. After you type your password once, sudo remembers it for about 15 minutes, so you do not have to keep retyping it. The list of users who are allowed to use sudo is controlled by a file called /etc/sudoers. On a Raspberry Pi, your default user (like 'youngster' or 'pi') is already in the sudo group, which means you can use it right away. You should never edit the sudoers file directly — if you make a mistake, you could lock yourself out. There is a special command called visudo that safely edits it, but you will not need that for a long time. The golden rule of sudo is: only use it when you actually need it. Do not put sudo in front of every command just because it works. If a command works without sudo, do not add it. Using sudo carelessly can change file ownership, overwrite important settings, or damage your system. Think of sudo like borrowing the master key to your school — you can open any door, but you should only open the ones you need.

commands.description: Runs whoami with superuser privileges. Instead of showing your username, it shows 'root' because the command runs as root.
Without sudo, whoami shows your regular username for comparison.
Updates the list of available software packages. This requires root access because it changes system files.

commands.description: Tries to read the password file without sudo. This will be denied because only root can read it.
With sudo, you can read protected system files. The shadow file stores encrypted passwords.
Shows which groups your user belongs to. You should see 'sudo' in the list, which is why you can use the sudo command.

challenge.question: Try running 'apt update' without sudo. What happens? Then run it with sudo. What is the difference?
challenge.hint: Without sudo, you will get a permission error. With sudo, it works because you are temporarily acting as root.

funFact: There is a famous comic from xkcd where someone asks a friend to make a sandwich. The friend says no. Then the person says 'sudo make me a sandwich' and the friend says 'okay.' That is how powerful sudo is!
